abstract: This lecture reviews inflammatory breast cancer (IBC), a rare but aggressive malignancy that accounts for 1, 5% of breast cancers and presents with rapid progression of erythema, swelling, and peau d'orange skin changes over weeks to months. Key diagnostic challenges include distinguishing IBC from mastitis, cellulitis, and other inflammatory conditions; a critical management principle is close follow-up (e.g., 2, 3 weeks) because IBC erythema expands quickly whereas infection improves with antibiotics. The lecture emphasizes that IBC often presents without a palpable mass, has a median age of 59, and carries a ten-year survival rate of about 18%, underscoring the need for timely biopsy and referral.
key_points: Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) accounts for 1, 5% of breast cancers and is rapidly progressive, often developing from zero to presentation over 3, 6 months.
The most common symptom of IBC is unilateral swelling or sensation of heaviness in the breast (79% of cases); the primary presenting sign is erythema.
It is uncommon to palpate a mass in IBC because the pathology involves tumor emboli blocking dermal lymphatics, causing skin thickening and peau d'orange without a discrete tumor.
Large axillary and infraclavicular nodes should be palpated; IBC often presents at stage III or IV (60, 70% of cases).
The ten-year survival rate for IBC is approximately 18%, similar to ovarian cancer, but IBC progresses much faster.
A key management pearl: when mastitis is suspected but IBC is possible, start antibiotics and schedule close follow-up (e.g., 2 weeks) because IBC erythema rapidly worsens while infection improves.
The most common finding on ultrasound in IBC is skin thickening.

First-line treatment for IBC involves three stages: neoadjuvant chemotherapy to shrink tumor, then surgical removal (mastectomy), then post-mastectomy radiation, all delivered rapidly due to the aggressive course.

Differential diagnoses for IBC include mastitis (lactational and nonlactational), idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, radiation-induced inflammation, cellulitis, folliculitis, hidradenitis suppurativa, and breast abscess.

Mastitis typically presents with central erythema around the areola spreading outward, whereas IBC erythema is more diffuse and rapidly progresses to involve at least one-third of the breast within weeks.
